Question: Do earthquakes have an equivalent for exoplanets?
Old_Answer: Yes, an exoplanet with tectonic activity is discovered, the LHS 3844b located 45 light-years from Earth. Image: Scientists from the University of Bern discovered the material inside LHS 3844b flows from one hemisphere to the other causing volcanic and tectonic activity. The truth is that we would expect quakes to occur on any rocky planet (the biggest magnitude of Marsquake recorded was 5 R). The causes may vary: 1. Pulsating Quakes. This type of quake occurs on a planet with a dense atmosphere. The atmosphere causes the crust of the planet to expand and contract. The pressure changes when this happens, causing the crust to crack and rebound. If the cracks become too large, they can lead to a pulsating quake. 2. Rotational Quakes. A planet's rotation may cause its crust to bulge outwards. This creates tension between the upper and lower layers of the planet's crust. As the planet rotates, the stress increases until it becomes strong enough to rupture the rock. This leads to a rotational quake. 3. Tectonic Shaking. Tectonic shaking is similar to rotational oscillation except that it does not involve the entire planet. Instead, tectonic vibration only affects certain areas of the planet. It is believed that tectonic shaking occurs when two plates collide. One plate slides under another, creating friction. Friction heats the plates, which eventually breaks them apart. Once the plates separate, the resulting shock wave travels through the planet's mantle. 4. Volcanic Shaking. Volcanoes are one of the best ways for an object to lose heat. They create hot lava flows that travel through the planet's interior. When the lava hits the mantle, it produces a volcanic shake. 5. Crustal Shaking. Crustal shaking occurs when the top layer of the planet s crust moves relative to the underlying mantle. This movement causes the veil to vibrate, which results in a seismic event. That is, no matter where you are in the Universe, avoid tall buildings. footnotes

Old_Answer: That wasn’t the case, Alexander didn’t copy Cyrus the Great (Cyprus is an island, not a Persian king). Cyrus and the Persian kings after him followed practically the same tactic as other great Asian conquerors before him (like the Hittites, for instance): He let his vassal regions do what they liked with only two but huge obligations; pay taxes to him and provide military personnel on his request. In return, he let them live. That meant in practice that the occupied regions (Ionian Greeks, Phoenicians, Egyptians, etc) kept their distinctive culture but were frequently exhausted financially and the income of all ended in the Persian treasury (this is why from time to time they revolted). Alexander had a different policy. He treated the conquered peoples equally with the Macedonians being their king, not their conqueror. That is why he gave high-ranking positions to Persians, imposed mixed marriages, and mainly invested in the conquered regions. The money from the Persian treasury did not go to Aigai but was used for projects throughout his empire. The result was the movement of ideas and people, which created the cultural explosion of the Hellenistic period. Do you want to see the difference? This is the main tomb in the catacombs at Kom el Shoqafa, Alexandria, of the Early Roman period construction.
